1864.keyTakeaways: Keep the tool that injured you, its packaging and any manual, and act quickly: Georgia generally allows two years to sue (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and bars strict liability claims more than ten years after a product's first sale (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11(b)(2)), while South Carolina allows three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5)) with no repose period. Georgia holds the manufacturer strictly liable for a defective tool, but not a seller that did not make it (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11.1). South Carolina holds any seller of a defective, unreasonably dangerous product strictly liable, retailers included (S.C. Code § 15-73-10). CPSC estimates about 30,600 emergency-room table saw blade-contact injuries a year (2010-2021 data), 96.4 percent of them to the finger in its 2017 study. The CDC reports about 36,000 emergency-room visits a year for chainsaw injuries.

faqs.question: Which garage tool causes the most serious injuries?
faqs.answer: The table saw is arguably the most dangerous tool a person can own. Its high-speed rotating blade presents a risk of laceration and amputation, and CPSC estimates about 30,600 emergency-room blade-contact injuries a year (2010-2021 data); in 2017, about 2,800 of 26,500 were amputations.

faqs.question: What injuries do common power tools cause?
faqs.answer: Tool-related accidents can result in amputation, puncture wounds, brain injury, broken bones, burn injuries and even death. The severity is often out of proportion to how routine the task felt.

faqs.question: Why do safety mechanisms not prevent these injuries?
faqs.answer: Because most injuries are direct hand contact with the blade: in CPSC's 2017 study, 96.4 percent of table saw blade-contact injuries involved the finger, and CPSC found no downward trend from 2004 to 2021 despite blade guards and riving knives. That is why CPSC has proposed requiring blade-stopping technology.

faqs.question: Can I bring a claim if a defective tool injured me?
faqs.answer: You may be able to. Where a tool was defectively designed or manufactured, or lacked adequate warnings, a product liability claim can target the manufacturer: in Georgia the manufacturer is strictly liable (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11); in South Carolina any seller of a defective, unreasonably dangerous product is (S.C. Code § 15-73-10). Preserve the tool exactly as it is after the injury.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a product liability claim in Georgia or South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Georgia generally allows two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), but no strict liability action may be brought more than ten years after the product's first sale (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11(b)(2)), and that bar also covers negligence claims against the manufacturer, with narrow exceptions (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11(c)). South Carolina allows three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5)), running from when you knew or reasonably should have known of the claim (S.C. Code § 15-3-535), and has no statute of repose for product claims. Keeping the tool, its packaging and any manual is what makes such a claim provable.

Table of Contents
  • Common Reasons Insurance Companies Deny Claims
  • Step 1 — Request and Review the Denial Letter
  • Step 2 — Gather Additional Evidence
  • Step 3 — Ask for Reconsideration in Writing
  • Step 4 — File a Complaint With Your State Insurance Regulator
  • Step 5 — File a Personal Injury Lawsuit
  • Bad Faith Denial Laws in Georgia
  • Bad Faith Denial Laws in South Carolina
  • GA vs. SC Comparison Table
  • Statute of Limitations — Don't Wait Too Long
  • Contact Roden Law

Getting a denial letter from an insurance company after a serious injury feels like a gut punch. You did everything right — reported the accident, sought medical treatment, filed a claim — and the insurer still said no. A denial is common enough that both states regulate how insurers handle claims.

But a denial is not the final word. Under both Georgia and South Carolina law, you have legal rights and concrete steps you can take to challenge an unfair denial. Bad faith, in the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School's definition, is dishonesty in a transaction — here, an insurer refusing to deal fairly with a claim. Whether your claim involves a car accident, a truck wreck, or a slip and fall on someone else's property, knowing how to respond to a denial can make the difference between walking away empty-handed and recovering the compensation you deserve.

This guide walks through the most common reasons claims get denied, the five steps you should take after receiving a denial, and the bad faith and claims-handling laws in Georgia and South Carolina, including whom each one protects.

Common Reasons Insurance Companies Deny Claims

Before you can effectively challenge a denial, you need to understand why it happened. Insurance adjusters rely on a handful of common justifications when denying personal injury claims. Some are legitimate coverage issues. Many are not.

Disputed liability. The insurer claims their policyholder was not at fault, or argues that you share enough blame to reduce or eliminate the claim. In states like Georgia, where the modified comparative fault threshold under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 bars recovery at 50% or more fault, adjusters will aggressively push the narrative that you caused the accident.

Lapsed or insufficient coverage. The at-fault driver's policy may have lapsed before the accident, or the policy limits may not cover the full extent of your injuries. This is especially common in motorcycle accident claims where injuries tend to be severe and medical costs run high.

Pre-existing conditions. A common denial ground. The insurer reviews your medical records, finds a prior injury to the same body part, and argues your current pain is simply a flare-up rather than a new injury caused by the accident. Georgia and South Carolina both follow the "eggshell plaintiff" doctrine, meaning a defendant takes the victim as they find them — but that does not stop insurers from trying.

Gaps in medical treatment. If you waited weeks or months before seeing a doctor, or if you missed follow-up appointments, the adjuster will argue that your injuries were not serious enough to warrant compensation. This is a particularly common problem in traumatic brain injury claims, where symptoms like confusion and headaches may not prompt an immediate ER visit.

Missed deadlines. Filing a claim after the policy's notification deadline or failing to provide requested documentation on time gives the insurer a procedural reason to deny the claim outright.

Recorded statement issues. If you gave a recorded statement to the insurance adjuster without legal counsel, anything you said — even casual, offhand remarks like "I'm doing fine" — may be used to undermine the severity of your injuries.

Step 1 — Request and Review the Denial Letter

The first thing to do after a denial is get the reason in writing. In Georgia an insurer must put a denial in writing and, if its policyholder asks in writing, explain the basis for it (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(10)). No statute gives a claimant against another driver's insurer that right in either state, so ask for the reasons in writing regardless. If you received a verbal denial over the phone, send a written request demanding the specific reasons for the denial, the policy provisions they relied on, and any documentation they reviewed.

Once you have the denial letter, read it carefully. Pay close attention to:

  • The specific reason or reasons cited for the denial
  • Any policy exclusions or limitations referenced
  • Any deadline the letter sets for a response or for additional information
  • The adjuster's name, claim number, and contact information

The denial letter is the roadmap for your entire response strategy. If the insurer says liability is disputed, you know you need stronger evidence proving fault. If they cite a gap in treatment, you need medical records explaining why. Every denial has a weak point — the letter tells you where to look.

Keep every piece of correspondence. Save emails, photograph letters, and note the date, time, and content of any phone calls. This paper trail becomes critical evidence if the case escalates to a bad faith claim or a lawsuit.

Step 2 — Gather Additional Evidence

Once you understand the basis for the denial, your next move is building a stronger case. The insurer denied your claim because they believe the evidence supports their position. Your job is to prove them wrong.

Medical records and expert opinions. If the denial is based on disputed injuries or pre-existing conditions, get a detailed narrative report from your treating physician explaining the causal connection between the accident and your current condition. For complex injuries — spinal cord damage, internal organ injuries, or traumatic brain injuries — an independent medical examination from a specialist can be particularly persuasive.

Accident reconstruction. When liability is disputed, accident reconstruction experts can analyze physical evidence, vehicle damage, road conditions, and witness statements to establish how the collision occurred and who was at fault. This is especially valuable in commercial truck accident cases where multiple parties may share responsibility.

Surveillance and documentation. Dashcam footage, security camera recordings from nearby businesses, and photos taken at the scene can contradict the insurer's version of events. Witness statements from people who were not involved in the accident carry significant weight as well.

Financial documentation. Gather every receipt, bill, and statement related to your injuries. Medical bills, pharmacy records, physical therapy invoices, lost wage documentation from your employer, and receipts for out-of-pocket expenses all strengthen the damages portion of your claim.

Step 3 — Ask for Reconsideration in Writing

There is no formal appeal of a liability insurer's denial in Georgia or South Carolina: you are not a party to the at-fault driver's policy, so a reconsideration letter is a request, not a procedure. Its force is the evidence it carries and the lawsuit it precedes. This is your chance to submit all the new evidence you have gathered and directly address each reason cited in the denial letter.

A strong reconsideration letter should:

  • Reference the claim number, denial date, and specific denial reasons
  • Present new or additional evidence that contradicts the denial
  • Cite the relevant policy language that supports coverage
  • Include supporting documentation — medical records, expert reports, witness statements
  • Set a deadline for the insurer to respond — in Georgia motor-vehicle cases an attorney-prepared pre-suit offer must allow at least 30 days to accept (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1); South Carolina sets no fixed period

Having an attorney draft or review the letter sends a clear message to the insurance company that you are serious about pursuing the claim.

If the insurer will not reconsider, the next steps involve taking the fight outside the insurance company's walls.

Step 4 — File a Complaint With Your State Insurance Regulator

When an insurance company denies a valid claim without a reasonable basis, or fails to properly investigate before issuing a denial, that conduct may violate the state's claims-handling laws. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 38-59-20) both prohibit unfair claim practices, and both states have regulatory agencies that accept consumer complaints.

In Georgia, you can file a complaint with the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire. In South Carolina, complaints go to the South Carolina Department of Insurance. These agencies require the insurer to answer the complaint in writing, can make it investigate thoroughly, and can take enforcement action — in South Carolina, cease-and-desist orders and penalties (S.C. Code § 38-59-30) — when claims-handling laws are broken. They do not decide what your claim is worth or order the insurer to pay it.

A regulatory complaint also puts the insurer's conduct on record. Regulators act on patterns — South Carolina's statute reaches practices carried out often enough to be a general business practice — so a complaint that joins others can bring enforcement your own case never would. It does not create a bad-faith claim for you against the other driver's insurer.

This step is particularly relevant in cases involving wrongful death claims, where families are grieving and insurance companies sometimes exploit the emotional burden to push lowball offers or outright denials.

Step 5 — File a Personal Injury Lawsuit

If reconsideration fails and the insurer refuses to offer fair compensation, filing a lawsuit may be the only remaining option. In both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to pursue a civil claim against the at-fault party. If the denial came from your own insurer — an uninsured or underinsured motorist claim, for example — you may also have a bad-faith claim against it. You cannot sue the other driver's insurer for bad faith in either state (Mills v. Allstate; Kleckley); when that insurer wrongly refuses to settle within its limits, the claim belongs to its own policyholder, who can assign it to you.

Filing a lawsuit does not necessarily mean going to trial. According to the Bureau of Justice Statistics, only about 4 percent of tort cases in a 2005 national sample of state courts ended in a trial; the rest ended by settlement, dismissal or other disposition. The act of filing signals to the insurance company that you are prepared to let a jury decide the case, which often prompts more serious settlement discussions.

Once a lawsuit is filed, discovery lets your attorney depose the at-fault party and witnesses, subpoena records, and test the facts the insurer relied on. A denial built on a thin file has to hold up under that scrutiny, which is often what moves the case toward settlement.

In medical malpractice cases and premises liability claims, the disputes are usually about duty and causation, which are decided on evidence a lawsuit can develop.

Bad Faith Denial Laws in Georgia

Georgia's bad-faith statute is a policyholder's remedy against their own insurer — on a denied med-pay claim, for example — not an injured person's remedy against the other driver's carrier. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, when an insurer refuses to pay a covered claim in bad faith and the insured is forced to litigate, it owes a penalty of up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

To trigger bad faith penalties under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, the policyholder must send a written demand for payment to the insurer at least 60 days before filing suit. If the insurer still refuses and the refusal is found to be in bad faith, the penalties apply on top of the underlying claim amount. On uninsured motorist claims the parallel rule is O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(j): a 60-day demand and a penalty of up to 25% or $25,000, whichever is greater, plus fees.

Georgia courts define bad faith as a frivolous and unfounded refusal to pay (Taylor v. Government Employees Ins. Co., 350 Ga. App. 734 (2019)); an insurer with a reasonable basis for its position does not owe the penalty even if it loses. Refusing to pay without a reasonable investigation is separately an unfair claims settlement practice the Commissioner can act on (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(6)).

Workers' compensation claims follow their own rules. In Georgia the insurer must start income benefits or file a notice to controvert within 21 days of learning of the injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-221); late benefits carry a 15 percent penalty, and an insurer that starts paying has 60 days from the first payment's due date to controvert. The State Board can assess attorney's fees against an insurer that defends without reasonable grounds (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-108), and there is no separate bad-faith lawsuit for a delayed comp claim.

Bad Faith Denial Laws in South Carolina

South Carolina addresses insurance bad faith through both statutory and common law. S.C. Code § 38-59-20 lists improper claim practices, including failing to acknowledge and act promptly on claims, failing to adopt reasonable standards for investigating claims, and not attempting in good faith to settle claims where liability is reasonably clear. The list expressly covers third-party liability claims, but it is enforced by the Director of Insurance against practices frequent enough to be a general business practice, and it gives no one a private claim.

South Carolina gives policyholders two remedies of their own. An insurer that refuses to pay its policyholder's claim for 90 days after a demand, without reasonable cause or in bad faith, owes attorney's fees capped at one-third of the judgment (S.C. Code § 38-59-40). And in the landmark case Nichols v. State Farm, the South Carolina Supreme Court recognized that insureds can sue their own insurer for bad faith refusal to pay benefits. Successful bad faith claims in South Carolina can result in compensatory damages, consequential damages, and in cases of egregious conduct, punitive damages.

Because the Nichols remedy is a tort claim, a policyholder's recovery is measured by the harm the denial caused rather than by a percentage of the claim. Punitive damages are available for willful or reckless conduct, capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed each year — $739,245 for 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).

This is an important consideration in pedestrian accident claims and motorcycle accident cases in South Carolina when the at-fault driver is uninsured or underinsured: the denied claim is then the UM/UIM claim against the injured person's own insurer, which is the claim Nichols protects.

Statute of Limitations — Don't Wait Too Long

Every personal injury claim is subject to a filing deadline, and a denied insurance claim does not pause or extend that deadline. If you spend months going back and forth with the insurance company and the statute of limitations expires before you file a lawsuit, you lose your right to sue — permanently.

Georgia: 2 years. Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, you have two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia. It can sneak up on claimants who are focused on the insurance process rather than the litigation timeline.

South Carolina: 3 years. Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, South Carolina allows three years from the date of injury to file suit. While this gives claimants more time, three years passes quickly when you factor in medical treatment, insurance negotiations, and requests for reconsideration.

There are narrow exceptions that may toll (pause) the statute of limitations in certain circumstances — for example, if the injured person is a minor or if the defendant left the state. But relying on exceptions is a dangerous strategy. The safest approach is to consult an attorney well before any deadline approaches.

This is particularly urgent for time-sensitive claims. In car accident cases where the denial comes several months after the accident, you may have less than a year left to file. In wrongful death cases, the Georgia statute of limitations is still two years from the date of death — not from the date of the denial.

The comparative fault rules add another layer of urgency. In Georgia, if a jury finds you were 50% or more at fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, you recover nothing. In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%. An experienced attorney can assess the liability picture early and build a strategy to counter the insurer's fault arguments before the clock runs out.

Contact Roden Law — We Fight Denied Claims

A denied personal injury claim does not mean your case is over. It means the insurance company made a business decision — and that decision can be challenged, overturned, or taken before a jury. At Roden Law, we represent injured people across Georgia and South Carolina who have been unfairly denied the compensation they are owed. Our attorneys understand the claims process, the reconsideration strategies that work, and the bad faith laws that hold insurers accountable when they refuse to do the right thing.

We handle every case on a contingency fee basis. You pay nothing unless we recover money for you. If you have received a denial letter and are not sure what to do next, call us for a free consultation.

Call 1-844-RESULTS or contact us online to speak with an attorney about your denied claim. We have offices in Savannah, Darien, Charleston, Columbia, and Myrtle Beach — and we are ready to fight for you.

Table of Contents
  • The General Rule: Personal Injury Settlements Are Usually Tax-Free
  • What Parts of a Settlement Are Not Taxable?
  • What Parts of a Settlement May Be Taxable?
  • Tax Considerations Specific to Georgia
  • Tax Considerations Specific to South Carolina
  • How Settlement Wording Affects Taxes
  • Common Case Types Where Tax Issues Arise
  • Steps to Protect Your Financial Recovery
  • How an Attorney Can Help With Settlement Taxes
After a serious accident, one of the first questions injury victims ask is whether they will owe taxes on their settlement or verdict award. The answer depends on the type of damages you receive, how your settlement is structured, and which state's laws apply to your claim. For residents of Georgia and South Carolina, understanding these rules is critical to keeping more of the money you deserve. The Internal Revenue Code § 104(a)(2) provides the foundational federal rule, but state-level tax treatment and how the settlement is written also play important roles.

The General Rule: Personal Injury Settlements Are Usually Tax-Free

Under federal law, compensation received "on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness" is excluded from gross income under IRC § 104(a)(2). This means the majority of a typical car accident, truck accident, or slip and fall settlement is not taxable at the federal level. The IRS treats these payments as making the injured person whole rather than providing new income — you are being reimbursed for losses you already suffered, not earning a profit. This exclusion applies regardless of whether you receive a lump sum settlement, a structured settlement paid over time, or a jury verdict. It also applies whether the case settles before trial, during trial, or after an appeal. The key factor is always whether the payment compensates for a physical injury or physical sickness.

What Parts of a Settlement Are Not Taxable?

Most categories of personal injury damages are excluded from taxation. Understanding which components are tax-free helps you appreciate the full value of your recovery:

Medical Expenses

Compensation for past and future medical bills — including hospital stays, surgeries, rehabilitation, prescription medications, and ongoing therapy — is not taxable. This applies to treatment for injuries from car accidents, motorcycle crashes, and all other personal injury claims. However, if you previously deducted medical expenses on your tax returns and then receive reimbursement through a settlement, those previously deducted amounts may be taxable under the "tax benefit rule."

Pain and Suffering

Non-economic damages for physical pain and emotional suffering caused by a physical injury are tax-free. Georgia and South Carolina both allow recovery for pain and suffering, and these awards — which often represent the largest portion of a settlement — remain fully excluded from income under IRC § 104(a)(2).

Property Damage

Reimbursement for vehicle repairs, replacement costs, and damage to personal property is not taxable. These payments restore you to your pre-accident position rather than providing income. If the reimbursement exceeds your adjusted basis in the property (what you originally paid), the excess could technically be a taxable gain, but this is rare in personal injury cases.

Loss of Consortium

Compensation paid to a spouse for loss of companionship, affection, and support resulting from the injured person's physical injuries is generally not taxable when it originates from a physical injury claim.

Wrongful Death Proceeds

Settlements and verdicts in wrongful death cases are generally tax-free under IRC § 104(a)(2) because they arise from a physical injury (the death). Compensatory damages recovered under Georgia's wrongful death statute (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1) and South Carolina's (S.C. Code § 15-51-10) are excluded from federal income tax; a South Carolina jury's exemplary damages under S.C. Code § 15-51-40 are punitive and remain taxable.

What Parts of a Settlement May Be Taxable?

While most personal injury compensation is tax-free, several categories of damages are potentially taxable. Understanding these distinctions before you settle can save you thousands of dollars:

Lost Wages and Lost Earning Capacity

Lost wages and lost earning capacity that are part of a physical-injury settlement are excluded along with the rest of the recovery under IRC § 104(a)(2). According to the IRS, compensatory damages, "including lost wages, received on account of a personal physical injury are excludable from gross income." Lost wages become taxable only when the underlying claim is not a physical injury, such as an employment claim for wrongful termination or discrimination (IRS Publication 4345), or lost profits of a business.

Emotional Distress (Without Physical Injury)

If you receive compensation for emotional distress that does not originate from a physical injury, the award is taxable. However, if your emotional distress stems directly from a physical injury — for example, anxiety and depression following a traumatic brain injury — the compensation remains tax-free. The distinction matters: emotional distress from witnessing an accident (without personal physical injury) is taxable, while emotional distress caused by your own injuries is not.

Punitive Damages

Punitive damages are taxable even when they arise from a physical-injury claim; the one exception in the Code (IRC § 104(c), for states whose wrongful death law allows only punitive damages) does not apply in Georgia or South Carolina. These damages are intended to punish the defendant rather than compensate the plaintiff, and the IRS treats them as income. In Georgia, punitive damages are capped at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), while South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed for inflation each year — $739,245 in 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530). Even though they arise from a personal injury case, punitive damages must be reported as "Other Income" on your federal tax return.

Interest on Settlement Awards

Pre-judgment and post-judgment interest added to your award is taxable as ordinary income. Even if the underlying damages are tax-free, any interest component is reported as interest income. In Georgia, a judgment earns post-judgment interest at the federal prime rate plus 3% (O.C.G.A. § 7-4-12), and pre-judgment interest is available only after a formal written demand under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-14; the 7% legal rate in O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2 does not govern tort judgments. In South Carolina, a judgment earns the prime rate plus four percentage points, compounded annually (S.C. Code § 34-31-20(B)). Whatever the rate, the interest is taxable.

Previously Deducted Medical Expenses

If you itemized medical expenses on a prior year's tax return and later receive a settlement reimbursing those same expenses, the reimbursed amount may be taxable under the tax benefit rule. You only need to include the amount that provided a tax benefit in the prior year.

Tax Considerations Specific to Georgia

Georgia conforms broadly to federal tax law for personal injury settlements, but several state-specific factors affect your case:
  • No state income tax on excluded damages: Georgia follows the federal IRC § 104(a)(2) exclusion, so damages excluded at the federal level are also excluded from Georgia state income tax (Georgia starts from federal adjusted gross income, O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27).
  • State income tax on taxable portions: Georgia's income tax is a flat 4.99% for 2026 (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20, as amended by HB 463), which applies to taxable components such as punitive damages and interest.
  • Modified comparative fault: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule — you can recover if you are less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your percentage of fault. The reduced amount remains subject to the same tax rules.
  • Statute of limitations: Georgia allows 2 years to file a personal injury claim (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Filing promptly ensures you preserve the right to recover tax-free compensation.
  • Workers' compensation exclusion: Workers' compensation benefits in Georgia are entirely tax-free under both federal and state law, including temporary total disability and permanent partial disability payments.

Tax Considerations Specific to South Carolina

South Carolina's tax treatment of personal injury settlements has some important differences:
  • State income tax conformity: South Carolina generally follows federal tax treatment for personal injury settlements, meaning amounts excluded under IRC § 104(a)(2) are also excluded from SC state income tax (S.C. Code § 12-6-40; from tax year 2026, South Carolina also starts from federal adjusted gross income).
  • Graduated state income tax: For 2026, South Carolina taxes income of $30,000 and above at 5.21% (1.99% below that) under H. 4216, slightly higher than Georgia's 4.99%.
  • Modified comparative fault: South Carolina uses a modified comparative fault system where you can recover damages if you are less than 51% at fault, providing slightly more latitude than Georgia's 50% threshold.
  • Longer filing deadline: South Carolina allows 3 years to file personal injury claims (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).
  • Workers' compensation: South Carolina workers' compensation benefits are also fully tax-exempt at both the federal and state level.
  • Punitive damages cap: SC caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, indexed each year ($739,245 in 2026) under S.C. Code § 15-32-530. These remain fully taxable regardless of the cap.

How Settlement Wording Affects Taxes

How the settlement is written matters for the parts of a recovery that can be taxed. An experienced personal injury attorney can negotiate settlement terms that maximize your after-tax recovery:

Allocate Damages Carefully

The settlement agreement should clearly allocate payments to specific damage categories. Stating what each part of the payment is for (medical expenses, pain and suffering, lost income from the injury, and separately any punitive damages or interest) gives the IRS a record to follow. The IRS respects reasonable allocations agreed upon by the parties, but may challenge allocations that appear designed solely to avoid taxes.

Consider a Structured Settlement

Instead of receiving a lump sum, you may negotiate a structured settlement that pays compensation over time through an annuity. Structured settlements offer several tax advantages: the investment income earned within the annuity is tax-free (unlike a lump sum invested independently), payments can be tailored to your financial needs, and the arrangement provides long-term financial security. This is particularly valuable in cases involving spinal cord injuries or brain injuries requiring lifetime care.

Separate Physical and Non-Physical Claims

If your case involves both physical injury claims and related non-physical claims (such as a defamation claim arising from the same incident), negotiating separate settlement amounts for each helps make clear that the physical injury compensation remains tax-free while only the non-physical portion is taxed.
Damage Type Federal Tax Georgia Tax South Carolina Tax
Medical expenses Not taxable Not taxable Not taxable
Pain and suffering Not taxable Not taxable Not taxable
Property damage Not taxable Not taxable Not taxable
Lost wages (from the physical injury) Not taxable Not taxable Not taxable
Emotional distress (from physical injury) Not taxable Not taxable Not taxable
Emotional distress (no physical injury) Taxable Taxable Taxable
Punitive damages Taxable Taxable (4.99%) Taxable (up to 5.21%)
Interest on award Taxable Taxable (4.99%) Taxable (up to 5.21%)
Workers' comp benefits Not taxable Not taxable Not taxable

Common Case Types Where Tax Issues Arise

Tax considerations affect settlements across all practice areas, but certain case types present more complex tax questions:
  • Truck accident claims — often involve large settlements with significant lost wage components (excluded when they flow from the injury), plus potential punitive damages against trucking companies that violated federal regulations.
  • Wrongful death cases — generally tax-free, but any punitive damage component and interest on a judgment remain taxable.
  • Medical malpractice claims — may involve large future medical expense awards that are tax-free, and future lost earning capacity is excluded along with them.
  • Workers' compensation cases — benefits are entirely tax-free, but if you receive both workers' comp and Social Security Disability, the combined amount may trigger taxation of a portion of your SSDI benefits.
  • Product liability cases — frequently include punitive damage claims against manufacturers, making settlement allocation especially important.
  • Premises liability claims — typically straightforward since most damages compensate for physical injuries, but commercial property claims may include taxable business interruption damages.

Steps to Protect Your Financial Recovery

Taking proactive steps before and during settlement negotiations can help you minimize your tax liability:
  1. Keep detailed medical records: Comprehensive documentation of your physical injuries strengthens the argument that all damages flow from a physical injury and should be tax-free.
  2. Track all medical expenses: Know exactly which medical costs you have deducted on prior tax returns to anticipate the tax benefit rule.
  3. Negotiate settlement allocation language: Ensure the settlement agreement specifies how the total amount is allocated among damage categories.
  4. Consider consulting a tax professional: If any part of your recovery is taxable (punitive damages, interest, or previously deducted medical expenses), a CPA or tax attorney can tell you how to report it and whether estimated payments are needed.
  5. Evaluate structured settlement options: For large awards involving lifetime care needs, structured settlements can provide significant tax savings over a lump sum.
  6. File on time: In Georgia, you have 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and in South Carolina, 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) to file your claim. Missing these deadlines eliminates your right to any recovery — taxable or otherwise.

How an Attorney Can Help With Settlement Taxes

An experienced personal injury lawyer does more than negotiate a fair settlement amount — they structure the agreement to protect your financial recovery from unnecessary taxation. At Roden Law, our attorneys understand which parts of a recovery can be taxed, write settlement agreements that state what each payment is for, and will point you to a tax professional for anything that must be reported. We handle personal injury cases across Georgia and South Carolina on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing unless we recover compensation for you. If you have been injured in an accident and want to understand the full value of your claim, including tax implications, contact Roden Law for a free consultation or call 1-844-RESULTS.

If you drive through North Charleston, you probably already know the intersection of Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 feels dangerous. What you may not know is that data confirms it: 629 crashes were recorded there between 2011 and 2015 — roughly one every three days, and more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties. Statewide it ranked second for 2011–2015, behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia; in 2024 it ranked fifth. Notably, none of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured (Post and Courier 2017 analysis of preliminary South Carolina Department of Public Safety data, 2011–2015).

As personal injury lawyers who handle crash cases from this intersection regularly, we've seen the injuries it produces — from T-bone collisions to rear-end chain reactions. Here's what makes this intersection so crash-prone and what you can do to protect yourself.

The Numbers: Ashley Phosphate & I-26 by the Data

Let's put the danger in perspective:

  • 2024 (latest state data): 174 collisions at I-26 and Ashley Phosphate Road — second in Charleston County and the tri-county behind I-26 at US-78 (190) and fifth statewide. No one was killed; 39 people were injured, and 148 of the crashes were property damage only (SCDPS 2024 Fact Book)

5 Reasons This Intersection Is So Crash-Prone

1. Interstate Speed Meets Red Lights

Vehicles exiting I-26 at Exit 209 come off the interstate and reach a signal at Ashley Phosphate Road a short distance later. Drivers who are distracted, unfamiliar with the area, or simply carrying too much speed can run the red light. The resulting T-bone collision with a vehicle legally entering the intersection produces catastrophic force.

2. Complex Left-Turn Movements

Ashley Phosphate Road has multiple left-turn lanes in both directions. Vehicles turning left must cross three lanes of opposing traffic on a seven-lane road. The margin for error is razor-thin — misjudge the gap by even one second and the result is a violent head-on-angle collision combining the energy of both vehicles.

3. Commercial Density Around the Interchange

Shopping centers, hotels, gas stations, and restaurants line Ashley Phosphate Road around the interchange. Drivers aren't just passing through — they're turning, merging, exiting parking lots, and hunting for entrances. This constant churn of turning movements creates unpredictable conflicts that even attentive drivers struggle to anticipate.

4. Drivers Who Fail to Yield

According to the SCDPS 2024 Fact Book, failure to yield the right of way was the leading contributing factor in Charleston County collisions in 2024. Where off-ramp traffic, left turns, and driveway traffic all meet, one driver who fails to yield can cause a collision.

5. Volume Has Outgrown Design Capacity

According to SCDOT, traffic on Ashley Phosphate Road has grown beyond the recommended level for two-way left-turn lanes. North Charleston's population reached about 129,245 in July 2025 (Census estimate), and I-26 carries 170,500 vehicles a day between Ashley Phosphate Road and Aviation Avenue, with 65,000 more on Ashley Phosphate Road (SCDOT, 2025).

Common Crash Types at Busy Interchanges

Crash TypeTypical CauseCommon Injuries
T-bone (side impact)Red-light running from I-26 off-rampPelvic fractures, internal organs, TBI
Left-turn collisionMisjudged gap in opposing trafficHead-on force injuries, chest trauma
Rear-end chainSudden stops at signal during congestionWhiplash, disc herniation, concussion
Pedestrian strikeTurning vehicles vs. pedestrians in crosswalkFractures, traumatic brain injury, fatality

What Should Be Done About It

Traffic engineers have tools that could reduce the crash frequency at Ashley Phosphate/I-26:

  • Protected left-turn signals — Eliminating permissive left turns during high-volume periods
  • Red-light cameras — A federal study found about 25% fewer right-angle crashes but about 15% more rear-end crashes; South Carolina law currently bars local camera ticketing (S.C. Code § 56-5-710(B))
  • Extended deceleration lanes — Giving I-26 exit traffic more distance to slow before reaching the signal
  • Restricted access management — Reducing the number of driveway access points near the intersection
  • Raised medians — SCDOT broke ground in July 2025 on an Ashley Phosphate Road safety project (Rivers Avenue to Dorchester Road) adding raised medians, high-visibility crosswalks, and better lighting

SCDOT has begun with that raised-median project; until more of these improvements are in place, crashes here are likely to continue.

What to Do If You're Injured at This Intersection

  1. Call 911 — Get a police report documenting the scene, signal state, and contributing factors
  2. Get medical treatment immediately — Trident Medical Center (9330 Medical Plaza Dr) is the closest trauma facility
  3. Photograph everything — Signal positions, vehicle damage, intersection layout, your injuries
  4. Get witness contacts — Nearby businesses may have seen the crash; get names and numbers before they leave
  5. Do not give recorded statements — The other driver's insurance company will try to minimize your claim
  6. Contact a lawyer — A Charleston car accident lawyer can pull traffic camera footage, obtain the signal timing report, and preserve evidence before it's lost

Your Legal Rights Under South Carolina Law

If you were injured at Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26:

  • Statute of limitations: 3 years from the date of injury to file suit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
  • Comparative fault: You can recover damages if you were less than 51% at fault — your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility
  • Government liability: If a malfunctioning or defective traffic signal contributed to your crash and the responsible agency knew or should have known and did not fix it, SCDOT or another agency may be liable under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(15)) — highway design itself is immune, and damages are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (S.C. Code § 15-78-120). These claims also have their own deadline: suit within two years, or three years if a verified claim is filed with the agency within one year (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-110, 15-78-80); filing that claim is optional
  • No upfront cost: Roden Law works on contingency — you pay nothing unless we recover compensation for your injuries

Free Case Review

Roden Law's North Charleston office on Spruill Avenue has handled dozens of cases from the Ashley Phosphate/I-26 intersection. We understand the specific hazards, we know where the evidence is (traffic cameras, business surveillance, signal data), and we have the resources to take these cases to trial if the insurance company won't pay fairly.

Call (843) 612-6561 or fill out our online form for a free, no-obligation case evaluation.

Types of Liens That Can Affect Your Personal Injury Settlement in Georgia and South Carolina

Table of Contents
  1. What Is a Lien on a Personal Injury Settlement?
  2. Medical Provider Liens
  3. Health Insurance Liens and Subrogation Rights
  4. Government Liens — Medicare, Medicaid, and VA
  5. Workers' Compensation Liens
  6. Attorney Liens
  7. Georgia vs. South Carolina Lien Rules — Comparison
  8. How to Negotiate and Reduce Liens on Your Settlement
  9. How a Personal Injury Lawyer Protects Your Settlement
  10. Contact Roden Law Today

After a car accident, trucking collision, or any serious injury caused by someone else's negligence, you might assume that the settlement check your attorney secures is entirely yours to keep. In many cases, however, third parties hold legal claims against a portion of that money. These claims are called liens, and they can reduce the amount you actually take home by thousands — or even tens of thousands — of dollars.

Both Georgia and South Carolina allow specific categories of lien holders to recover money from personal injury settlements. Understanding which liens apply, how they work under each state's laws, and how to negotiate them down is critical to protecting your compensation. For background on lien law generally, see the Legal Information Institute's overview of liens.

What Is a Lien on a Personal Injury Settlement?

A lien is a legal right held by a third party to claim a portion of your settlement or verdict proceeds. When you receive medical treatment, government benefits, or workers' compensation payments after an injury, the entities that paid those costs often have a statutory or contractual right to be reimbursed from any recovery you receive from the at-fault party.

Liens can come from hospitals, health insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, the VA, workers' compensation carriers, and even your own attorney. In both states a valid lien follows the settlement money, and your attorney must hold disputed funds in trust until it is resolved.

The key distinction is between a statutory lien — created by state or federal law — and a contractual lien — created by an insurance policy or provider agreement. Statutory liens carry the force of law and are harder to negotiate. Contractual liens, while enforceable, sometimes offer more room for reduction.

If you were injured in a truck accident or motorcycle crash that required extensive hospitalization, the total lien amount can be substantial. Cases involving traumatic brain injuries or spinal cord injuries often generate six-figure medical bills — and corresponding liens that must be addressed before you see a dime.

Medical Provider Liens

Medical provider liens are among the most common liens in personal injury cases. Hospitals, physicians, and other treatment providers can claim part of your settlement to recover the cost of care they provided for your injuries.

Georgia Hospital Liens

Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470, a hospital, nursing home, or physician, chiropractic or burn-care practice that treats you has a lien on your claim for the reasonable charges for that care, subordinate to your attorney's lien.

To perfect it, the provider must give written notice at least 15 days before filing a verified statement with the superior court clerk — within 75 days after discharge for hospitals, or 90 days after first treatment for physician and chiropractic practices. Since July 1, 2023, the lien is unenforceable unless the provider first billed your health insurer. Georgia hospital liens do not apply to workers' compensation claims — only to third-party liability recoveries — and cannot include charges for unrelated conditions.

South Carolina Hospital Liens

South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute. A hospital or doctor there cannot file a lien against your claim; its right to be paid rests on your contract with it, including any assignment of benefits or letter of protection you signed, and is enforced like any other bill. The claims that do reach a South Carolina settlement are health-insurer subrogation, Medicaid, Medicare and workers' compensation, each covered below.

Doctor and Physician Liens

In Georgia, physician and chiropractic practices hold the same statutory lien as hospitals, under the 90-day rule above. In South Carolina, a doctor's claim is contractual — typically a letter of protection under which the doctor agrees to wait for payment until the case resolves — and contractual claims tend to be more negotiable than statutory liens. The enforceability of a physician lien depends on the specific language of the signed agreement and whether the provider followed proper procedures.

Health Insurance Liens and Subrogation Rights

If your health insurer paid for injury-related treatment, it may have a right to be reimbursed from your settlement, within statutory limits in both states. This right is called subrogation, and it functions much like a lien.

Subrogation works like this: your insurer pays your medical bills, then steps into your shoes and demands reimbursement from your settlement. The legal basis is usually found in the insurance policy's subrogation or reimbursement clause.

Georgia Subrogation Rules

Georgia codifies the "made whole" doctrine in O.C.G.A. § 33-24-56.1: a health or disability insurer may be reimbursed only if your recovery exceeds all of your economic and noneconomic losses, and even then its claim is reduced by a pro rata share of your attorney's fees and expenses. If your settlement does not fully cover your medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering, the insurer has no right of reimbursement.

A Georgia-regulated policy cannot contract around this rule. The exceptions are plans state law cannot reach: self-funded employer (ERISA) plans, federal-employee plans, Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE. A self-funded ERISA plan's own terms control, but it can reach only the settlement fund itself.

South Carolina Subrogation Rules

South Carolina's protection is statutory. Under S.C. Code § 38-71-190, a health insurer may subrogate only if the policy provides for it and only up to what it paid, must pay its share of fees and costs, and can be barred by the Director of Insurance from inequitable subrogation. The type of health insurance you carry — private, employer-sponsored, ERISA, or government — plays a major role in determining how much of your settlement a health insurer can claim.

Government Liens — Medicare, Medicaid, and VA

Government liens are the most powerful and least negotiable category of liens in personal injury cases. Federal law gives Medicare, Medicaid, and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) recovery rights that state law cannot cut off, although federal law also caps what Medicaid can take.

Medicare Liens

Under the Medicare Secondary Payer Act (42 U.S.C. § 1395y(b)), Medicare must be repaid from any liability settlement, judgment or award, whether or not it mentions medical expenses. This federal right overrides state lien and made-whole rules and can be reduced, waived or compromised only through Medicare's own procedures; CMS does not pursue physical-trauma liability settlements of $750 or less. Medicare Advantage plans assert the same secondary-payer recovery rights (42 C.F.R. § 422.108).

Medicare's lien applies to conditional payments — bills Medicare paid on the condition that it be repaid if a liable party later pays. According to CMS, its recovery center lists the payments it considers related, lets you dispute unrelated charges, and after settlement issues a formal demand; repayment is due within 60 days, interest runs from the demand date, and unpaid debts go to the Treasury for offset. If funds are paid out first, Medicare can collect from you or your attorney, and double damages are possible if the government must sue. The demand is reduced by Medicare's share of your attorney's fees and costs.

Medicaid Liens

Both Georgia and South Carolina Medicaid programs have statutory rights to recover payments from personal injury settlements. Georgia's Medicaid lien authority comes from O.C.G.A. § 49-4-149, while South Carolina's derives from S.C. Code §§ 43-7-430 and 43-7-440. Like Medicare, Medicaid liens are backed by federal law (42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(25)) and cannot simply be ignored.

However, in Arkansas Dept. of Health & Human Services v. Ahlborn (2006), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Medicaid can only assert a lien against the portion of a settlement representing medical expenses — not the entire recovery. This ruling provides a basis for reducing Medicaid liens, especially when non-medical damages like pain and suffering make up the bulk of the settlement. Later decisions refined the rule: a state cannot simply presume that a fixed share of the recovery is medical (Wos v. E.M.A., 2013), but it may recover from the portion allocated to future as well as past medical care (Gallardo v. Marstiller, 2022).

VA Liens

Veterans treated by the VA, and service members and families on TRICARE, may face a federal recovery claim under the Federal Medical Care Recovery Act (42 U.S.C. § 2651) and 38 U.S.C. § 1729. The United States can recover the reasonable value of the care from the at-fault party or its insurer.

Workers' Compensation Liens

When a workplace injury involves a negligent third party — such as a commercial truck driver who causes a crash while you are on the job — you may receive both workers' compensation benefits and a third-party settlement. The workers' compensation carrier then has a lien on your third-party recovery.

Georgia Workers' Compensation Liens

Under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11.1, a Georgia workers' compensation insurer that has paid benefits to an injured worker is entitled to a lien on any recovery the worker obtains from a negligent third party. The lien covers the disability, death and medical benefits actually paid, but it is enforceable only if the carrier proves you have been fully and completely compensated for all economic and noneconomic losses, counting both the comp benefits and the third-party recovery.

If the carrier does recover, the court may apportion a reasonable attorney's fee between your lawyer and the carrier's lawyer by the work each did.

South Carolina Workers' Compensation Liens

S.C. Code § 42-1-560 governs workers' compensation liens in South Carolina. The carrier's lien is on the recovery net of the fees and expenses of obtaining it. Notice of suit goes to the Commission, employer and carrier within 30 days, and the suit must be started within one year after the carrier accepts liability or pays under an award, or the claim can pass to the carrier. If a settlement is less than your total damages, the Commission can cut the lien proportionally.

Workers' compensation liens are particularly relevant in slip and fall cases that occur on a job site, construction injuries involving third-party contractors, and motor vehicle accidents that happen during the course of employment.

Attorney Liens

Your own attorney also has a claim on the proceeds for fees and costs — the attorney's lien, which differs by state.

Georgia Attorney Liens

Georgia recognizes both charging liens and retaining liens under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14. A charging lien gives the attorney a claim against the settlement proceeds obtained through the attorney's efforts. In personal injury cases, it secures the contingency fee set in your written fee agreement plus any case costs advanced by the attorney.

South Carolina Attorney Liens

South Carolina has no attorney's-lien statute. Its courts recognize a common-law lien for costs the attorney advanced; a lien for the fee itself exists only if your written fee agreement creates one (Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co.).

In Georgia the attorney's lien outranks every lien except tax liens, and hospital and Medicaid liens are expressly subordinate to it; Medicare is not subordinate but reduces its demand for fees and costs.

Georgia vs. South Carolina Lien Rules — Comparison

Georgia and South Carolina lien rules differ in several key ways, as the side-by-side comparison below lays out.

Lien Type Georgia South Carolina
Hospital Lien Statute O.C.G.A. §§ 44-14-470 to 44-14-477 None; providers rely on contract
Hospital Lien Filing Deadline 75 days after discharge (hospitals); 90 days after first treatment (physician/chiropractic); 15 days' prior notice Not applicable
Made Whole Doctrine Codified (O.C.G.A. § 33-24-56.1); policy cannot override; self-funded ERISA and federal plans exempt No case law; S.C. Code § 38-71-190 limits subrogation
Workers' Comp Lien Statute O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11.1 S.C. Code § 42-1-560
Workers' Comp Fee Reduction Lien only if worker fully compensated; court apportions fee Lien net of fees and costs; Commission may reduce
Attorney Lien Statute O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14 No statute; common-law lien for costs; fee lien by written agreement
Medicaid Lien Authority O.C.G.A. § 49-4-149 S.C. Code §§ 43-7-430, 43-7-440
Statute of Limitations (PI) 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
Comparative Fault Standard Modified — barred if 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) Modified — barred if 51% or more at fault

These differences matter in practice. A Georgia lien that misses the notice or filing rules is invalid, except against a liable party or insurer that had actual notice of it before settling, and comparative fault findings reduce your total settlement — which also reduces what lien holders can collect. In Georgia, you are barred from recovery if you are 50% or more at fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. In South Carolina, the threshold is slightly more favorable — you can recover as long as your fault stays below 51%.

How to Negotiate and Reduce Liens on Your Settlement

Most liens can be reduced. Some reductions are written into the statutes; others come from challenging the lien's validity or amount. Here are the primary strategies:

Challenge the Lien's Validity

If a Georgia provider missed the filing deadline, included charges for unrelated treatment, failed to serve the correct parties, or never billed your health insurer first, the lien may be invalid. Your attorney should review every lien for procedural defects before agreeing to pay anything.

Apply the Made Whole Doctrine

In Georgia, the complete-compensation rule eliminates a health insurer's reimbursement claim if your settlement does not fully compensate you; in South Carolina, you can petition the Director of Insurance to disallow inequitable subrogation. This argument is especially powerful in catastrophic injury cases — such as those involving traumatic brain injuries or spinal cord damage — where the total damages far exceed the available insurance coverage.

Request a Compromise from Government Lien Holders

Medicare reduces its demand for your attorney's fees and costs, and you can request a waiver or compromise, with detailed documentation of the case value and the reasons a full recovery was not possible, or appeal the amount. South Carolina Medicaid must cut its claim by 25 percent when you hired a lawyer and may compromise the rest; Georgia Medicaid is limited to the medical-expense share of the recovery.

Negotiate with the Workers' Compensation Carrier

Workers' compensation carriers frequently agree to reduce their liens in exchange for faster resolution. Many will accept an additional reduction beyond the statutory fee offset rather than risk losing their recovery entirely at trial.

Use the "Common Fund" Doctrine

This doctrine holds that a lien holder who benefits from the attorney's efforts should bear a proportionate share of fees and costs. For most liens the share is written into the statute: Georgia health insurers, Medicare, and South Carolina workers' compensation carriers, health insurers and Medicaid all recover net of fees and costs, and the reduction generally tracks your actual fee rather than a fixed one-third.

How a Personal Injury Lawyer Protects Your Settlement

The difference between an attorney who aggressively negotiates liens and one who pays them at face value can be tens of thousands of dollars in your pocket. Here is what an experienced personal injury attorney does to protect your recovery:

  • Identifies all liens early. Your attorney tracks every potential lien holder — hospitals, insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, workers' comp carriers — and obtains lien amounts before settlement negotiations begin.
  • Audits lien amounts for accuracy. Medical provider liens often include billing errors or charges for unrelated treatment. Your attorney reviews every line item and challenges anything that does not belong.
  • Negotiates reductions. Most lien holders accept less than the full amount when presented with a well-documented request.
  • Applies legal protections. Georgia's made whole rule, South Carolina's subrogation limits, and statutory fee reductions work in your favor — but only if your attorney raises them.
  • Ensures proper distribution. Settlement funds are held in trust and distributed according to lien priority. Failing to properly satisfy liens can expose both you and your attorney to legal liability.

This applies across all injury types — car accidents, medical malpractice, wrongful death, and beyond. Lien resolution is also time-sensitive. Georgia's two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's three-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) mean that delays from unresolved liens can put your entire case at risk.

1711.keyTakeaways: Liens from hospitals, health insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, workers' compensation carriers, and attorneys can significantly reduce your personal injury settlement. Georgia's provider lien statute (O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470) lets hospitals and medical practices place a lien on your claim; South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute, so providers there rely on contract. Federal liens from Medicare (42 U.S.C. § 1395y) take priority over state law. Workers' comp liens are governed by O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11.1 in Georgia and S.C. Code § 42-1-560 in South Carolina. An experienced attorney audits every lien, challenges invalid or unrelated charges, and applies every statutory reduction the lien holder must accept.

faqs.question: What is a lien on a personal injury settlement?
faqs.answer: A lien is a legal claim against your settlement or judgment by a third party who paid for expenses related to your injury. Common lien holders include hospitals, health insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, workers' compensation carriers, and attorneys. Valid liens must be satisfied before you receive your share of the settlement proceeds.

faqs.question: Can hospital liens reduce my personal injury settlement in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's hospital lien statute (O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470) allows hospitals to place liens on personal injury settlements for the reasonable cost of treatment. The lien attaches to any recovery from a third-party claim. However, these liens are often negotiable, and your attorney can work to reduce the amount owed.

faqs.question: How do medical liens work in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute, so a hospital or doctor cannot file a lien against your claim. A provider's right to be paid rests on your contract with it — including any assignment of benefits or letter of protection you signed — and it is negotiated like any other bill. The claims that do reach a South Carolina settlement are health-insurer subrogation (allowed only if your policy contains a subrogation clause, S.C. Code § 38-71-190), Medicaid (§§ 43-7-430, 43-7-440), Medicare, and workers' compensation (§ 42-1-560).

faqs.question: Does Medicare have a lien on my personal injury settlement?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under the Medicare Secondary Payer Act (42 U.S.C. § 1395y(b)), Medicare must be repaid the conditional payments it made out of any liability settlement, judgment or award, and its right overrides state law. Repayment is due within 60 days of Medicare's demand, with interest after that, and Medicare can collect from you or your attorney if the money is paid out first — so the Medicare claim must be resolved before funds are distributed.

faqs.question: Can my attorney negotiate liens to increase my take-home amount?
faqs.answer: Yes. Experienced personal injury attorneys routinely reduce liens by challenging invalid or unrelated charges, invoking Georgia's complete-compensation rule or South Carolina's statutory limits on health-insurer subrogation, applying the federal rule that limits Medicaid to the medical-expense share of a recovery, and using Medicare's fee-reduction, waiver and compromise procedures.

faqs.question: What happens if I ignore a lien on my settlement?
faqs.answer: Ignoring a valid lien has serious consequences. Insurers, workers' compensation carriers and Medicaid can sue to recover what they are owed (in Georgia, a hospital enforces its lien against the at-fault party or its insurer), and your attorney must hold disputed funds in trust until the claims are resolved. Medicare charges interest on unpaid demands, refers unpaid debts to the U.S. Treasury for offset, and can collect from your attorney; in South Carolina, continued Medicaid eligibility depends on cooperating with the agency's reimbursement claim.
